title: Called to beatitude (CCC 1716–1729)
hook: the beatitudes describe the happiness God wants for us

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christian funerals: the Church walks with the dead to the grave and hands them over to God. Your line was commended to God. Who did you remember? Today a new part begins: how Catholics live. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

The part of the Catechism about how Catholics live could have gone straight to a list of rules. It doesn't. Long before the commandments, it turns to a mountain, a crowd, and one word said again and again: blessed. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are they that mourn. Jesus sits down, his disciples come close, and before any instruction about what to avoid, he describes people who are, in his word, blessed. Some of them don't look blessed at all. The grieving. The ones who hunger and thirst. The ones being persecuted. So the moral life in this book turns, first, on a surprise about who is happy. Today's word is the call underneath it.
screen: `NOT A LIST OF RULES.` → `BLESSED, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THE GRIEVING, THE PERSECUTED.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls the beatitudes the heart of Jesus's preaching. In the Douay-Rheims Bible the first one reads: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Some readers hear the word blessed as happy, and that's close to the point the Catechism makes next. It says the beatitudes answer the natural desire for happiness, and that this desire comes from God, placed in the human heart to draw people to himself. Saint Augustine, quoted right there, puts it as a question to God: how is it that I seek you? Because in seeking you, I seek the happy life. So in this telling, morality doesn't start with what's forbidden. It starts with what a person wants most, and with the claim that God wants it for them too. Then the beatitudes turn that wanting around. True happiness, the Catechism says, isn't found in riches or comfort, in fame or power, or in any human achievement, however useful. It names the goal in other words: the coming of the kingdom, the vision of God, entering into God's rest. "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And it adds something about the beatitudes themselves: they show the face of Jesus Christ. They describe him first, the poor one, the meek one, the one who mourned, and then they describe the happiness held out to anyone who follows. So the question shifts. Not only what am I allowed to do, but what am I made for. The Catechism says the beatitudes put decisive choices in front of a person. Everything in this part of the book, the commandments included, comes after that.
screen: `THE HEART OF JESUS'S PREACHING.` · `A DESIRE FOR HAPPINESS, FROM GOD.` · `NOT RICHES, FAME OR POWER.` · `THE FACE OF CHRIST.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your deepest desire. Settle, and breathe. Start with the surface wants: a quieter week, a reply to a message, a bit more money. Let them come, and let them go by. Then ask underneath: if I had all of those, what would I still want? Keep asking until you reach something you can't buy. Maybe to be known. To be at peace. To love someone well. Name it in a few words, silently. If you pray, you can hold that desire up to God and leave it there. If you don't, just stay with it, without fixing anything. The bell holds the time.
Called to beatitude. Beatitude means blessedness, a happiness that comes as a gift. The Catechism says the human person is called to it, and that the beatitudes show the way. Today's word.
Your line: made for happiness. Today, when you catch yourself chasing something, ask once: is this the happiness I'm made for, or a stand-in for it? Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the beatitudes from Matthew 5 read at Mass, and the Catechism places them near the start of its teaching on the moral life, before the commandments.

fork.setup: a friend asks where a guide to how Christians live ought to begin. by the Catechism's own order, what comes first?
options: with the rules that must never be broken.
with the happiness people are made for.
with a checklist of good habits.
fork.reveal: the Catechism's part on the moral life opens with human dignity, and almost at once turns to the beatitudes and the call to beatitude. the commandments come later.

original.note: Greek: blessed, happy — the word that opens each beatitude in Matthew 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy word for being lucky.
what it means: the happiness God made people for, described in the beatitudes and lived by Jesus.
what a scholar hears: makarioi in Matthew's Greek, beati in the Latin, and Augustine seeking the happy life by seeking God.

notes: CCC 1716–1729 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): heart of Jesus's preaching (1716), the face of Christ (1717), natural desire of divine origin (1718), kingdom, vision of God, God's rest (1720), not in riches, fame, power (1723), decisive choices (1723/1726). Confirm paragraph references.
Augustine's line paraphrased from the Catechism's quotation of Confessions 10.20; Pusey 1838 could be quoted if a Keeper supplies the exact wording.
